q-139469.name: Question 1
q-139469.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
q-139469.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\,\,\,\,\cdot \,[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{90}[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(1-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(-3-(-1))^{2}+(-3-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0+4+9} \\  & =\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx. In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[−2−1−22120−1]⟹AT=[−2−210−122−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[−2−1−22120−1]⋅([−2−210−122−1]⋅[−2−1−22120−1])−1⋅[−2−210−122−1]⋅[12−3−3]=[−2−1−22120−1]⋅[90010]−1⋅[−90]=[−2−1−22120−1]⋅190[10009]⋅[−90]=[−2−1−22120−1]⋅[−10]=[22−10]=x^

Finally, the distance between x and the subspace S is given by d(x,x^)=‖x−x^‖=(x1−x^1)2+(x2−x^2)2+(x3−x^3)2+(x4−x^4)2=(1−2)2+(2−2)2+(−3−(−1))2+(−3−0)2=1+0+4+9=14.

q-139473.name: Question 2
q-139473.problem:
Find the distance between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
q-139473.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{16}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-3)^{2}+(6-1)^{2}+(4-(-1))^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+25} \\  & =\sqrt{50} \\  & =5\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-86829.name: Question 3
q-86829.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Round the answer to $2$ decimal places.
q-86829.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,3\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot (-4)}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{24}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{3\cdot 8}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{8}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{8}}{3})≈{19.47}^{∘},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

q-40578.name: Question 4
q-40578.problem:
Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-40578.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors

$\,$ $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,2\,{\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Computing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 1+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{\pi }{3},
$$

which is already an acute angle.

q-81435.name: Question 5
q-81435.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
q-81435.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to its row echelon form. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-40619.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
q-40619.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}$ are free variables. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is the basis of the solution space of the system.

Now, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
